A more extensive writeup of the results from this task is available as a separate technical report published by ORNL. 1.2.3 Applications and Process Window The application and process window for AMEC looks to be quite broad but has primarily been tested by Skuld at various foundry locations such as their own facility or at Ohio State University. To prove the capability, and also showcase it in a mobile capacity, Skuld helped ORNL restore a mobile foundry developed by the US Army and housed within two shipping containers. ORNL inherited the mobile foundry from Rock Island Arsenal in early 2025 in a non-working state (Figure 4). The foundry was originally configured with a furnace for aluminum, a furnace for steel, sand mixing, shaking, and blasting equipment for patterns, and a large chiller. The sand-handling equipment was removed as it was not needed for the AMEC process. With help from the team at Skuld, the systems within the container including furnaces, chiller, and other auxiliary equipment, were able to be repaired and returned to an operational state. Figure 4: Mobile foundry unit during repairs and restoration. In addition to restoring the foundry container, ORNL staff needed training on how the AMEC process works and how to conduct general foundry activities. A team of five engineers from ORNL traveled to Skuld’s Ohio foundry for three days of classroom and hands-on training. The team learned how to assemble a casting pattern with gates, vents, and down sprue, how to properly coat the pattern with a ceramic slurry, how to setup barrels with sand and bury the casting pattern, and finally how to melt and pour the metal safely over the 3D printed pattern. Another critical component of the training was operational safety and proper personal protective equipment (PPE). At the end, each team member had successfully cast a bevel gear from aluminum (Figure 5). Figure 5: The ORNL team with completed castings at the Skuld facility. With the mobile foundry operational and the team members trained, it was time to take the system on the road and test new applications for the AMEC process. ORNL sent the mobile foundry to Schofield Barracks in Hawaii to work directly with the US Military as part of a larger exercise for expeditionary manufacturing training. There were two goals for the exercise: gain additional experience and knowledge of using the AMEC process in an expeditionary environment and demonstrate knowledge transfer of the AMEC and foundry processes to enlisted military personnel.
